title: The ALM Proxy is a generic call executor, so every safety property must be enforced by the controller before doCall is reached
content:
Both Aave flows execute through the same primitive. The operator must "encode the `approve` function call, using `abi.encodeCall`" and then "send the encoded call using `proxy.doCall()` specifying the `address` of the `asset` contract" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.2.1.3.1.6.1/.6.2); the supply call, and the withdraw call on the pool, follow the identical encode-then-`doCall` shape (.3.1.7.2, .3.2.6.2).

`doCall` is therefore an arbitrary-call façade: given a target address and a calldata blob it will execute it from the proxy's account. It contributes no validation of its own.

That places the entire security boundary in the controller function that constructs the payload. `onlyRole(RELAYER)`, `isActive`, the `rateLimited` modifier and the hardcoded `address(proxy)` recipient are all properties of `depositAave` / `withdrawAave`, not of the proxy. The proxy is powerful and unopinionated; the controller is the thing that makes it safe.

The practical implication for review and for governance is sharp: auditing the proxy tells you almost nothing about Spark's risk posture. What matters is the exhaustive set of controller functions permitted to call `doCall` and the guards each one carries. Any newly added controller function is a new hole in the perimeter unless it independently reimplements all four constraints — which is exactly why the Artifact documents these process definitions guard-by-guard rather than as a single 'call Aave' instruction.
description: Deposits and withdrawals are abi.encodeCall payloads relayed through proxy.doCall, meaning the proxy itself imposes no semantics
